meaning: Takes a supposition or a known situation as a premise and draws a conclusion or asks a question: “supposing that...”, “if that is so, then...”; it can also open a sentence to pick up what the other person said.
connection: Verb / い-adjective plain form, な-adjective / noun (+ だ) + とすれば / としたら / とすると; sentence-initially: だとしたら / だとすれば / とすると

senses.label: Pure hypothesis
senses.meaning: Imagines a situation that may not be real, then states the result: “supposing ...”, “if ... were ...”. Often paired with 「仮に」 or 「もし」. The three forms mean almost the same; 「としたら」 is the most conversational.
senses.connection: Plain form + としたら／とすれば (common: 仮に〜としたら, もし〜とすれば)
examples: Supposing you won the lottery, what would you spend it on?
If I could be reborn, I'd want to be a bird.

senses.label: Reasoning from a known fact
senses.meaning: Takes something you heard or saw as a premise and draws a logical conclusion: “if so, then ...”. The second half often ends in 「〜はずだ」, 「〜ことになる」, or 「〜だろう」. 「とすると」 is used most for this kind of reasoning.
senses.connection: Plain form + とすると／とすれば (「とすると」 or 「だとすれば」 can also open a sentence on its own)
examples: If he's the culprit, then the story adds up.
If the meeting ends at three, I should be able to leave the office by four.

senses.label: Followed by a question
senses.meaning: Sets up a premise, then asks a question or for an opinion: “if ..., then what / where ...?”. The second half usually has a question word like 「どこ」, 「いつ」, or 「何」.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form + としたら + question
examples: If you were to live abroad, which country would be good?
If I leave now, which train should I take?

senses.label: At the start of a sentence
senses.meaning: 「だとしたら」, 「だとすれば」 and 「とすると」 can start a sentence to reason from what the other person said: “in that case”.
senses.connection: Start of sentence + だとしたら／だとすれば／とすると、〜
examples: “I heard that restaurant is closed today.” “In that case, let's go somewhere else.”

notes: Only for assumptions or premises. Don't use it for something that will definitely happen: ✕「駅に着いたとしたら電話して」→ ○「駅に着いたら電話して」.
After 「とすると」 you can't put a command, request, or statement of will: ✕「行くとすると、早く準備しなさい」→ ○「行くとしたら／行くなら、早く準備しなさい」.
Saying 「あなたの話が本当だとすれば」 to someone signals “I'm not sure what you say is true”, so it can sound like you doubt them. If you just want to pick up their topic, 「〜なら」 is safer.
A noun or na-adjective normally needs 「だ」 first: ✕「本当とすれば」→ ○「本当だとすれば」.
Don't confuse it with 「〜ようとすると」 (just as one is about to ...): 「出かけようとすると、雨が降り出した」 means “just as I was about to go out”, not a hypothesis.

daily.title: Chatting about “what if”
daily.description: Friends talk about what they'd do in an imaginary situation.
daily.example: If you had a hundred million yen, would you quit your job?

daily.title: Solving a mystery drama
daily.description: Watching a detective show with family and discussing who did it.
daily.example: If that person is lying, then his alibi falls apart.

daily.title: Planning a trip
daily.description: Talking with family about where to go on vacation.
daily.example: If we travel over summer break, Hokkaido would be nice.

daily.title: Discussing a rumor
daily.description: You hear a friend is quitting their job.
daily.example: If he's really leaving the company, it'll be lonely around here.

work.title: Analyzing data in a meeting
work.description: Explaining a projection to colleagues based on known data.
work.example: If sales continue at this pace, we expect to hit our target by the end of the year.

work.title: News commentary
work.description: A commentator draws a conclusion from a news report.
work.example: If this report is true, it will probably become a serious problem.

work.title: Research paper
work.description: A paper proposes a hypothesis and reasons from it.
work.example: If this hypothesis is correct, the conventional explanation needs to be reconsidered.

etymology: Formed from the quoting particle 「と」 plus a conditional form of the verb 「する」 (here meaning “to assume, to suppose”). 「とすれば」 uses 「ば」, 「としたら」 uses 「たら」 and 「とすると」 uses the conditional 「と」. The sentence-initial 「だとしたら」, 「だとすれば」 and 「とすると」 first turn the other person's words into a statement and then treat it as a supposition.
formation: Formed from the quoting particle 「と」 + the verb 「する」 + a conditional form 「ば / たら / と」. Here 「する」 does not mean “do” but “regard as, set as” (as in 「AをBとする」); 「と」 presents the whole preceding clause as a proposition, so nouns and な-adjectives first take 「だ」 to make a full sentence (「本当だとすれば」). Literally it is “if we set ... as fact” — the first half is only “set up”, not a confirmed fact, so it naturally carries the nuance of a hypothesis or “taking ... as a premise for now”. This one core produces every sense here: setting up a situation that may not exist and stating the result (pure supposition); provisionally taking something heard or seen as true and drawing a logical conclusion (inference from a premise); setting a premise and then asking a question or for an opinion (before a question); and first turning the other person's words into a 「だ」 statement and then supposing it, which lets it open a sentence to pick up their words (sentence-initial use). The three conditional forms also keep their own character: 「たら」 is colloquial and casual, 「ば」 is more written and logical, and 「と」 expresses a natural result, so 「とすると」 suits “in that case it must follow that...” inferences best, and the main clause does not take commands or volition.

similar.title: 〜なら
similar.explanation: 「〜なら」 is typically used to pick up the other person's topic and give advice (「京都に行くなら、秋がいい」), and can be followed by will or requests. 「〜とすれば」 sets up your own premise and reasons from it; it is more logical in tone and isn't used to give advice.

similar.title: 〜たら
similar.explanation: 「〜たら」 can express a condition that is sure to happen (「駅に着いたら電話して」). 「〜としたら」 always means “let's suppose ...”: the premise is uncertain or contrary to fact, so it can't be used for something that will certainly occur.

similar.title: 〜となると・〜となれば・〜となったら
similar.explanation: Also built from 「と」 + a conditional form of a verb. 「〜となると」 means “once it actually comes to ...”, and the premise is usually something that is or is about to become real (「海外転勤となると、家族も大変だ」). The premise of 「〜とすれば」 is only a supposition and can be unrealistic.

similar.title: 〜としても
similar.explanation: Same origin: both come from 「と」 + 「する」 (“to assume”). 「〜としても」 is concessive, “even if we assume ... (the result doesn't change)” (「雨だとしても行く」); 「〜とすれば」 is straightforward, “if we assume ..., then ...”.

meaning: An emphatic form of 「もし」. It supposes something unlikely that might happen, or something contrary to fact: “if, by any chance, ...”, “in case ...”.
connection: もしも + verb ta-form + ら／noun・na-adjective + だったら (also works with 「ば」 or 「なら」)

senses.label: Just in case (worry)
senses.meaning: Supposes something unlikely but serious if it happens: “if by any chance ...”. Stronger than 「もし」, it stresses “in the unlikely event”, often with a note of anxiety.
senses.connection: もしも + 〜たら／〜ば／〜なら (common: もしも地震が起きたら, もしも何かあったら)
examples: If an earthquake should happen, first get under a desk.
If anything should happen to me, I want you to read this letter.

senses.label: Contrary to fact
senses.meaning: Imagines a situation that is the opposite of reality or impossible, to express a fantasy or regret: “if only ...”, “what if ...”. The second half often uses 「〜のに」 or 「〜だろう」.
senses.connection: もしも + noun・na-adjective + だったら／verb ta-form + ら
examples: If I were a bird, I could fly freely across the sky.
If I had chosen a different path back then, I probably wouldn't be who I am today.

senses.label: 「もしもの時」
senses.meaning: 「もしも」 can also act as a noun: 「もしもの時／もしもの場合」 means “in an emergency”, “just in case”. Common when talking about disaster preparation or insurance.
senses.connection: もしも + の + 時・とき・場合・こと
examples: Let's get water and food ready, just in case.
In case of emergency, please call this number.

notes: 「もしも」 does not express a condition by itself; it must be matched by 「たら／ば／なら」 later in the sentence: ✕「もしも雨が降る、中止です」→ ○「もしも雨が降ったら、中止です」.

「もしも」 carries the nuance of “a very unlikely, just-in-case possibility”. Saying 「もしも合格できたら」 about someone's good news may make them feel you think success is unlikely; for good wishes, plain 「合格したら」 is enough.
「もしものこと」 is a euphemism for death or misfortune. Saying 「もしものことがあったら」 to a sick person, an elderly person, or their family is considered very ill-omened (「縁起でもない」).
Don't use 「もしも」 for something that will naturally happen: ✕「もしも明日になったら」→ ○「明日になったら」.

daily.title: Warning a child
daily.description: A parent tells a child what to do in a dangerous situation.
daily.example: If a stranger ever talks to you, run away right away.

daily.title: Daydreaming
daily.description: Friends talk about things that could never happen.
daily.example: If you could use magic, what would you want to do?

work.title: Disaster training
work.description: Explaining emergency procedures at a company safety training.
work.example: In the event of a fire, please evacuate using the emergency stairs.

work.title: Explaining insurance
work.description: An insurance company introduces a product to a customer.
work.example: To be prepared for the unexpected, we recommend this insurance plan.

etymology: 「もし」 is an old adverb of supposition, used as the Japanese reading of the kanji 「若」 (“if”). Adding the emphatic particle 「も」 gives 「もしも」, which sounds stronger. The phone greeting 「もしもし」 is usually traced to 「申す申す」 (“I'm speaking, I'm speaking”), so it has a different origin.

similar.title: 〜たら
similar.explanation: 「もし〜たら」 is a general hypothesis; with 「も」 added, 「もしも」 stresses “just in case”, and is mostly used for things one doesn't want to happen, such as disasters and accidents, or very unlikely things. In everyday speech plain 「もし」 is enough.

similar.title: 〜とすれば・〜としたら・〜とすると
similar.explanation: 「仮に〜としたら」 also expresses a pure hypothesis, but it is more rational and detached, often used in discussion and reasoning (「仮に一億円あったとしたら」). 「もしも〜たら」 is more emotional, often with a tone of anxiety or imagination.

similar.title: もしかしたら〜かもしれない
similar.explanation: Same origin: both contain the hypothetical adverb 「もし」. 「もしかしたら〜かもしれない」 is not a conditional clause but a guess, “maybe ...” (「もしかしたら雨かもしれない」), whereas 「もしも〜たら」 is a conditional, “if by any chance ... (then ...)”.

formation: 「もしも」 is the hypothetical adverb 「もし」 + the emphasizing particle 「も」, and it is paired with a conditional form such as 「たら／ば／なら」. 「もしも」 does not form the condition itself; it merely announces at the start of the sentence that “a hypothesis follows”. The actual condition is carried by 「たら」 and the like, so the sentence still works without 「もしも」, whereas 「もしも」 without a conditional form is ungrammatical. The particle 「も」 adds a feeling of “even something like this”, which makes 「もしも」 stand out more than 「もし」 as “a very slim chance, but just in case”, hence its frequent use for disasters, accidents, and other unwelcome events. Because it condenses the sense of “a worst case”, 「もしも」 can even be used directly as a noun, as in 「もしもの時」 and 「もしものこと」.

meaning: “If you don't do something, a bad result will follow, or something won't be possible.” Often used to urge, remind, or state a necessary condition.
connection: Verb nai-form + と + second clause (bad result / negative)

senses.label: If not, something bad happens
senses.meaning: If you don't do something, a bad result will follow: “if you don't ..., you'll ...”. Often used to remind or hurry someone. The second half is usually negative, like 「遅れる」, 「困る」, or 「怒られる」.
senses.connection: Verb nai-form + と、〜 (common: 急がないと遅れる, 早く寝ないと)
examples: If you don't hurry, you'll miss the train.
If you don't take your medicine properly, you won't get better.
If I don't do it now, I'll be in trouble later.

senses.label: Can't ... unless ...
senses.meaning: States a necessary condition: if the first part isn't met, the second can't happen: “you can't ... unless ...”. The second half is usually a negative or a negative potential form.
senses.connection: Verb nai-form + と + 〜ない／〜できない (common: 予約しないと入れない)
examples: You can't get into this restaurant without a reservation.
You won't get good at it unless you practice every day.

senses.label: It has to be ...
senses.meaning: With the negative of nouns or adjectives, 「じゃないと／でないと」, it means “if it's not ..., it won't do”. It expresses a condition or a personal preference.
senses.connection: Noun・na-adjective + じゃないと／でないと; i-adjective く + ないと
examples: This is the only brand of coffee I can drink.
I can't concentrate on studying unless the room is bright.

notes: The second half is a “bad result” or “can't do”; it can't be a request, command, or statement of will: ✕「行かないと、連絡してください」→ ○「行けなかったら／行かないなら、連絡してください」.
The 「と」 in 「〜ないと思う」 and 「〜ないと言う」 is quotative: 「彼は来ないと思う」 means “I think he won't come”, not “if he doesn't come ...”. Misreading it gives the opposite meaning.
「急がないと遅れますよ」 and 「ちゃんとやらないと」 have a tone of reminding or lecturing, so to a superior or a customer they sound preachy. Use a softer phrasing such as 「お急ぎになったほうがよろしいかと思います」.
Nouns and na-adjectives take 「じゃないと／でないと」, and i-adjectives take 「〜くないと」: ✕「学生ないと」→ ○「学生じゃないと」, ✕「明るいないと」→ ○「明るくないと」.

daily.title: Hurrying the family
daily.description: A mother tries to get her child out of bed in the morning.
daily.example: If you don't get up now, you'll be late!

daily.title: Reminding a friend to take an umbrella
daily.description: Warning a friend about the weather before going out.
daily.example: If you don't take an umbrella, you'll get wet.

daily.title: Explaining your habits
daily.description: Telling a friend about your daily routine.
daily.example: If I don't eat breakfast, I have no energy.

work.title: Reminding about a deadline
work.description: Coworkers remind each other of a submission deadline.
work.example: If you don't apply by the end of today, they won't accept it.

work.title: Explaining a procedure
work.description: A clerk at the counter explains which documents are needed.
work.example: You can't open an account without ID.

etymology: Made of the negative 「ない」 plus the conditional particle 「と」. 「と」 originally expresses a natural consequence (“whenever A, B”); attached to a negative, it becomes “if not A, then B”.

similar.title: 〜ないといけない
similar.explanation: Same origin: add 「いけない」 after 「〜ないと」 and you get “must ...”. A sentence-final 「〜ないと。」 is an abbreviation of 「〜ないといけない」 (“I'd better ...”), whereas this grammar point sits mid-sentence and is followed by the result of “if not ...”.

similar.title: 〜なければならない
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: 「〜なければ」 also means “if not ...”, and with 「ならない」 it expresses obligation. 「〜なければ」 is more formal and written, and its second half is freer; 「〜ないと」 is colloquial, and its second half is mostly a bad result that follows naturally.

similar.title: 〜と (conditional)
similar.explanation: Same origin: this grammar point is the conditional 「と」 (“as soon as ...”) attached to a negative form. 「と」 expresses a necessary, natural result, so the second half of 「〜ないと」 likewise cannot take will, requests, or commands.

similar.title: 〜てからでないと
similar.explanation: Also built from 「でない」 + 「と」, but it means “unless you first do A, you can't do B”, stressing order (「予約してからでないと入れない」). 「〜ないと」 only says “if you don't, something bad will happen” and doesn't stress order.

formation: It is made of the negative auxiliary 「ない」 + the conditional particle 「と」. 「と」 expresses a condition where “once the first part holds, the second part inevitably follows” (「春になると暖かくなる」). Put a negative into the first part and you get “as long as you don't do ..., ... will inevitably happen”, so the second part is naturally a bad consequence or “can't do”. Since 「と」 states a rule-like inevitable result rather than the speaker's will, the second half cannot hold a request, command, or statement of will. When speakers use this “if not ..., then ...” form to alert someone, it takes on an urging tone; and if the latter half 「いけない」 is dropped, it becomes the sentence-final 「〜ないと。」 (“I've got to ...”).

meaning: Imagines a situation contrary to reality to express regret, disappointment, or frustration with someone: “if only ... (but it isn't so)”.
connection: Verb / adjective ba-form + 〜 + のに (noun・na-adjective: 〜なら〜のに)

senses.label: Regret about reality
senses.meaning: Supposes a condition that doesn't exist and states the good result that would follow, regretting that it isn't so: “if ..., then ... (but sadly not)”.
senses.connection: 〜ば、〜 (potential form・ta-form) + のに
examples: If I had money, I could buy this house.
If I were a little taller, I could have become a model.

senses.label: Regret about the past
senses.meaning: Expresses regret about something that already happened. 「〜ばよかったのに」 is common: about others it sounds like blame; about yourself it shows remorse.
senses.connection: 〜ばよかったのに／〜ば〜たのに
examples: You should have said so sooner.
If I had studied more, I could have passed.

senses.label: Complaint / suggestion
senses.meaning: 「〜ばいいのに」 tells someone “why don't you just ...?”, as a complaint or a soft suggestion. It can also express your own wish.
senses.connection: Verb ba-form + いいのに
examples: If you're that tired, you should just take a rest.
I wish the rain would stop.

notes: 「〜ばいいのに」 and 「〜ばよかったのに」 said to someone carry blame: “why didn't you ...?”. Even in honorific form (「早くおっしゃってくださればよかったのに」) it is very rude to a superior or customer; say 「事前にお知らせいただけると助かります」 instead.
Tense changes the meaning: 「もっと練習すれば勝てるのに」 is regret about the present (the match isn't over / you aren't practicing now); 「もっと練習していれば勝てたのに」 is regret about a loss that has already happened.
The first half must be contrary to fact or nearly impossible. For a simple supposition whose truth is unknown you can't end with 「のに」; use 「〜ば〜だろう」.
For nouns and na-adjectives use 「〜なら〜のに」 or 「〜だったら〜のに」: ✕「学生ば、割引があるのに」→ ○「学生なら、割引があるのに」.

daily.title: Seeing something expensive
daily.description: You like something in a store, but it's too expensive.
daily.example: If it were a little cheaper, I'd buy it.

daily.title: A friend tells you too late
daily.description: A friend tells you afterward that they had a problem.
daily.example: If you were in trouble, you should have come to me.

daily.title: Complaining about the weather
daily.description: It's raining on the weekend, and you grumble at the window.
daily.example: If it were sunny, we could have gone on a picnic.

work.title: Project review
work.description: Looking back after a problem in a project and expressing regret.
work.example: If we had checked more carefully beforehand, we could have prevented this mistake.

work.title: Grumbling among coworkers
work.description: Colleagues privately talk about company rules.
work.example: I wish meetings were shorter.

etymology: Made of the conditional 「ば」 and the contrastive particle 「のに」 (“even though”). When 「のに」 ends a sentence, the second half is left unsaid, leaving a feeling of “but in reality it isn't so”.

similar.title: 〜ばよかった
similar.explanation: Same origin: 「〜ばよかった」 is regret about your own past action; with 「のに」 added, 「〜ばよかったのに」 is mostly regret or blame aimed at someone else (“it would have been good if you had ...”).

similar.title: 〜のに (contrast)
similar.explanation: Same origin: the 「のに」 here is the concessive 「のに」 (“even though ...”). Mid-sentence, 「〜のに」 is followed by the second half (「勉強したのに落ちた」); this grammar point drops the “but reality is the opposite” half, leaving only the regret.

similar.title: 〜といい・〜たらいい (wish)
similar.explanation: Both 「〜といいのに」 and 「〜ばいいのに」 mean “it'd be nice if ...”. 「〜といいのに」 is mostly a simple wish or regret; 「〜ばいいのに」 about other people's actions more easily carries blame or urging.

similar.title: 〜だろうに
similar.explanation: 「〜だろうに」 also expresses regret that “it should have been ... but ...” (「言えば分かっただろうに」), but it is more written and often carries consideration or sympathy for someone else; 「〜ば〜のに」 is more colloquial and the emotion more direct.

formation: It is made of the hypothetical 「ば」 + a main clause + the concessive conjunctive particle 「のに」. The full meaning is “if ..., then ... would ..., but (in reality it isn't so)”. After 「のに」 there should be the half “but reality is the opposite”, yet both speakers already understand it, so it is dropped, leaving only the regret or dissatisfaction that 「のに」 carries. Because 「のに」 contrasts with “reality”, the first half must be a supposition contrary to fact, and the main clause is the result one “could have had”. Used about yourself it is remorse; used about others it becomes the blame “you could have ... but didn't”, which is why it is easy to be rude when you say it to someone.

meaning: Means you believe you did something (though maybe you didn't), or you treat something you didn't do as done: “I thought I had ...”, “pretend that ...”.
connection: Verb ta-form + つもり（だ／で／だった）; verb te-iru form + つもり

senses.label: Thought I had done it
senses.meaning: The speaker believes they did something, but reality may be different: “I thought I had ...”. Often 「〜たつもりだったが／のに」, showing a gap between belief and fact.
senses.connection: Verb ta-form + つもりだ／つもりだった（が）
examples: I thought I had locked the door, but it was open.
I thought I had explained it clearly, but it didn't get across.

senses.label: Pretend it's done
senses.meaning: You didn't actually do it but treat it as done, to console yourself or to save money: “pretend that ...”. Usually 「〜たつもりで」.
senses.connection: Verb ta-form + つもりで + second clause (common: 旅行に行ったつもりで, 買ったつもりで)
examples: I pretended I'd gone on a trip and saved that money instead.
I'll give it one more try, as if I had nothing left to lose.

senses.label: Believe yourself to be ...
senses.meaning: 「〜ているつもり」 means the speaker believes they are in a certain state, though others may not see it that way. Often used to be modest or to defend yourself.
senses.connection: Verb te-iru form + つもり (common: 分かっているつもり, 気をつけているつもり)
examples: I believe I understand it.
I thought I was taking care of my health, but I ended up in the hospital.

notes: Tense decides the meaning: 「行くつもりだ」 = “I intend to go” (future); 「行ったつもりだ」 = “I think I've gone / let's say I've gone”. Using the た form as “intention” changes the meaning entirely.
Saying 「彼は分かったつもりでいる」 about someone is sarcastic, “he thinks he's understood”; saying 「分かったつもりでしょう」 to their face is very rude.
After a mistake at work, saying 「ちゃんと確認したつもりです」 can be heard in Japan as shifting the blame. Apologize first: 「確認が不十分でした。申し訳ありません」.
「〜ているつもり」 (believing one is in some state) differs from 「〜るつもり」 (intend to): 「気をつけているつもり」 = “I believe I've been careful”; 「気をつけるつもり」 = “I intend to be careful from now on”.

daily.title: Worrying after leaving home
daily.description: After going out, you worry you left the gas on and tell your family.
daily.example: I think I turned off the gas, but I'm a little worried.

daily.title: Resisting the urge to shop
daily.description: You see something you like but decide not to buy it.
daily.example: Let's just pretend I bought it and hold back.

work.title: Checking on an email
work.description: A coworker says they didn't get your email, and you explain.
work.example: I thought I sent the email yesterday. Didn't you get it?

work.title: A new employee being modest
work.description: A new employee talks about their attitude toward work in a meeting with a manager.
work.example: I believe I have learned basic business manners.

etymology: 「つもり」 comes from the masu-stem of the verb 「積もる」 (to pile up; to estimate). It originally meant “estimate, calculation” and came to mean “intention, belief”. With the ta-form, it means “believing in your mind that something is done”.

similar.title: 〜つもりだ
similar.explanation: Same origin: 「dictionary form + つもりだ」 expresses an intention for the future (「来年留学するつもりだ」); with the た form it means “I take it that I've done it” or “let's say I did”. The same 「つもり」 changes meaning completely with tense.

similar.title: 〜つもりだった
similar.explanation: Same origin: 「〜つもりだった」 is “I had intended to (but didn't)”, whereas 「〜たつもりだった」 is “I thought I'd done it (but actually hadn't done it properly)”. The former is a plan that fell through; the latter is a perception that doesn't match the facts.

similar.title: 〜つもりで
similar.explanation: Same origin: 「〜つもりで」 is “doing something with the intention of ...” (「一生住むつもりで買った」); 「〜たつもりで」 is “treating it as if ... had been done” (「旅行したつもりで貯金する」).

similar.title: 〜ふりをする
similar.explanation: 「〜ふりをする」 is “pretending” for others to see (「寝たふりをする」); 「〜たつもり」 is a conviction inside oneself that doesn't necessarily show outwardly, and is often sincerely believed.

formation: It is the perfective 「た」 + the formal noun 「つもり」. 「つもり」 comes from 「積もる」 (to estimate); its core meaning is “what you have worked out in your mind”. After the dictionary form, what you've estimated is something to do in the future, i.e. “intention”; after the た form, what you've estimated is that “it's already done”, i.e. “I believe I did it”. 「つもり」 exists only in the mind and doesn't guarantee agreement with the facts, so 「〜たつもり」 often implies “in fact it wasn't done”, and is frequently followed by 「が」 or 「のに」. If you know you haven't done it but “count it” in your mind as done, it becomes “let's say I did ...” (「旅行したつもりで」). In the same way, with the 「ている」 form it means “I believe I'm in that state” (「分かっているつもり」).

meaning: Expresses a plan or intention you had in the past, usually implying things turned out differently: “I was going to ... (but)”, “I didn't mean to ...”.
connection: Verb dictionary form・nai-form + つもりだった; noun + の + つもりだった

senses.label: Was going to ..., but
senses.meaning: You had a plan, but it didn't happen or the situation changed: “I was going to ... (but)”. Often followed by 「が」, 「けど」, or 「のに」.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form + つもりだった（が）／つもりでいた（のに）
examples: I was planning to rest at home this weekend, but some work suddenly came up.
I was determined to go to bed early today, but I stayed up late again.

senses.label: Didn't mean to ...
senses.meaning: 「〜つもりはなかった」 means “I had no such intention”, used in apologies or excuses: “I didn't mean to ...”.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form + つもりはなかった／つもりはありませんでした
examples: I didn't mean to hurt you. I'm sorry.
I never intended to say something like that.

senses.label: Meant it as ...
senses.meaning: 「Noun + のつもりだった」 means “I meant it as ...”, but the other person took it differently. Often used to clear up a misunderstanding.
senses.connection: Noun + の + つもりだった (common: 冗談のつもりだった, 親切のつもりだった)
examples: I meant it as a joke, but she got really angry.
I meant it as a kindness, but it only caused trouble.

notes: 「行くつもりだった」 = “I was going to go” (probably didn't); 「行ったつもりだった」 = “I thought I'd gone”. Only 「た」 differs, but the meaning is completely different.
The position of the negative changes the meaning: 「行かないつもりだった」 = “I'd intended not to go” (but went); 「行くつもりはなかった」 = “I had no intention of going at all”, used to stress “it wasn't deliberate”.
When you've hurt someone, saying only 「傷つけるつもりはなかった」 or 「冗談のつもりだった」 will be taken in Japan as making excuses and dodging responsibility. First say 「申し訳ありません」, then explain what you meant.
A noun needs 「の」: ✕「冗談つもりだった」→ ○「冗談のつもりだった」.

daily.title: Explaining a no-show to a friend
daily.description: You planned to go to a party but couldn't make it.
daily.example: I was going to go, but I came down with a fever.

daily.title: Apologizing after an argument
daily.description: Apologizing after saying something that upset the other person.
daily.example: I didn't mean to make you angry.

work.title: Reporting a delay
work.description: Explaining to your boss why a plan wasn't finished.
work.example: I was planning to finish it this week, but it looks like it'll be a little late.

work.title: Explaining the wording of an email
work.description: Clearing up a misunderstanding with a client.
work.example: I did not mean to rush you. My apologies.

etymology: 「つもり」 is a noun made from the masu-stem of 「積もる」 (to estimate) and means an intention in your mind. With the past 「だった」, it means “a past intention”, which naturally suggests things turned out differently.

similar.title: 〜つもりだ
similar.explanation: Same origin: 「〜つもりだ」 is an intention that still holds now; in the past form 「〜つもりだった」 usually implies the intention fell through or circumstances changed, and it is often followed by 「が」 or 「のに」.

similar.title: 〜たつもり
similar.explanation: Same origin: 「〜たつもりだった」 is “I thought I'd done it” (「鍵をかけたつもりだった」), a perception that doesn't match the facts; this grammar point is “I originally intended to”, a plan that didn't come true.

similar.title: 〜(よ)うと思う
similar.explanation: 「〜ようと思っていた」 also expresses a past intention, leaning toward “I was thinking of ... at that time”, which is more casual and spontaneous; 「〜つもりだった」 expresses a plan decided beforehand and is more definite.

formation: It is the formal noun 「つもり」 (an intention in one's mind) + the past tense of the copula 「だった」. On the surface the past tense only says “I had that intention then”, but if the intention were still valid you would normally say 「つもりだ」; choosing the past implies that “this intention no longer holds”, which naturally brings out the sense of “it didn't go as planned / things changed”, often followed by 「が」 or 「のに」. Putting the negative after 「つもり」 (「つもりはなかった」) denies the “intention” itself, giving “I didn't mean to”; 「noun + のつもりだった」 means “I had cast it in my mind as ...”, often used to explain the other person's misunderstanding.

meaning: Means doing something with a certain intention, resolve, or mindset: “with the intention of ...”, “in the spirit of ...”.
connection: Verb dictionary form・nai-form + つもりで; noun + の + つもりで; その・この + つもりで

senses.label: With the intention of ...
senses.meaning: Doing an action with a certain plan or resolve: “intending to ...”, “determined to ...”. The second half is the action actually taken.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form・nai-form + つもりで + action
examples: I bought this house intending to live here for the rest of my life.
I left my hometown determined never to return.

senses.label: As ..., in the spirit of ...
senses.meaning: 「Noun + のつもりで」 means “as ...”, “treating it as ...”. It explains your real intention or attitude when doing something.
senses.connection: Noun + の + つもりで (common: 冗談のつもりで, 旅行のつもりで, 練習のつもりで)
examples: I only said it as a joke, but they took it seriously.
I took the exam just for practice.

senses.label: Be prepared for ...
senses.meaning: 「そのつもりで」 means “with that in mind”, “be prepared for that”. Often used to give someone advance notice.
senses.connection: その／この + つもりで（いてください／お願いします）
examples: We start early tomorrow morning, so please be prepared for that.
I think the meeting will run long, so plan your schedule with that in mind.

notes: 「行くつもりで」 = “with the intention of going”; 「行ったつもりで」 = “as if I had already gone”. The dictionary form and the た form mean completely different things.
When the other person is hurt, saying 「冗談のつもりで言ったんです」 will be taken in Japan as shifting the blame (implying they can't take a joke). Apologize first.
「そのつもりでいてください」 has a tone of giving instructions; to customers or superiors, say 「あらかじめご了承ください」 or 「その旨ご承知おきください」.
A noun needs 「の」: ✕「練習つもりで」→ ○「練習のつもりで」.

daily.title: Encouraging a friend
daily.description: A friend is about to play in an important match, and you cheer them on.
daily.example: Don't worry about losing. Just go out there and give it everything.

daily.title: Clearing up a misunderstanding
daily.description: You took a joke too far and explain what you meant.
daily.example: I didn't say that to make fun of you.

work.title: A reminder from the boss
work.description: A boss tells a team member in advance that next week will be busy.
work.example: Next week is going to be busy, so get ready with that in mind.

work.title: A new employee's resolve
work.description: A new employee speaks at their welcome ceremony.
work.example: I will do my very best, ready to learn everything from scratch.

etymology: 「つもり」 comes from the masu-stem of 「積もる」 (to estimate) and means an intention in your mind. Adding 「で」, which marks manner or state, gives “with this intention or mindset”.

similar.title: 〜つもりだ
similar.explanation: Same origin: 「〜つもりだ」 states an intention at the end of a sentence; 「〜つもりで」 treats the intention as the “frame of mind or premise” for what follows, so an actual action must follow.

similar.title: 〜たつもり
similar.explanation: Same origin: 「〜たつもりで」 is “as if ... had been done” (「旅行したつもりで、そのお金を貯金した」), when it actually wasn't; 「〜つもりで」 with the dictionary form is “intending to do”.

similar.title: 〜つもりだった
similar.explanation: Same origin: 「〜つもりだった」 looks back on a past intention and often implies it wasn't realized; 「〜つもりで」 is the frame of mind you hold while doing something, regardless of the result.

similar.title: 〜として
similar.explanation: 「Nとして」 is an objective status or capacity (「練習試合として行う」); 「Nのつもりで」 is a subjective frame of mind (「練習のつもりで受ける」), which others needn't share.

formation: It is the formal noun 「つもり」 (an intention or assumption in one's mind) + the case particle 「で」. Here 「で」 expresses the state or manner in which something is done (as in 「笑顔で」 and 「本気で」), so the “intention” becomes a state accompanying the following action: “doing ... with this intention”. Hence the first part is a frame of mind and the second part must be an action actually taken. Since 「つもり」 is a noun, it can take 「noun + の」, and 「Nのつもりで」 means “with the mindset of N”; 「そのつもりで」 uses 「その」 to refer to the arrangement just mentioned, meaning “with that in mind (and prepare accordingly)”.

meaning: Means deliberately putting on an appearance that isn't true: “pretend to ...”, “act as if ...”.
connection: Verb / i-adjective plain form, na-adjective + な, noun + の + ふりをする

senses.label: Pretend (action / state)
senses.meaning: Deliberately acting a certain way for others to see, when it isn't true: “pretend to ...”. Common phrases: 「寝たふり」, 「知らないふり」, 「見ないふり」.
senses.connection: Verb ta-form・te-iru form・nai-form + ふりをする (in speech 「を」 can drop: ふりして)
examples: I didn't want anyone to talk to me, so I pretended to be asleep.
He actually knows, but he's pretending not to.
It was a hassle, so I pretended not to hear and walked on by.

senses.label: Posing as someone
senses.meaning: 「Noun + のふりをする」 means posing as a certain person or role: “pretend to be ...”, “pose as ...”.
senses.connection: Noun + の + ふりをする
examples: Cases of people posing as police officers to swindle money are on the rise.
The children are playing doctor.

senses.label: Putting on a feeling
senses.meaning: With adjectives, it means faking a state or feeling: “act ...”, “pretend to be ...”. Often used to hide your true feelings.
senses.connection: i-adjective plain form／na-adjective + な + ふりをする
examples: I was actually sad, but I acted cheerful.
I pretended to be busy and got out of helping.

notes: 「ふりをする」 is pretending (when it's not the case). For merely imitating an action, use 「まねをする」: ✕「先生の話し方のふりをする」→ ○「先生の話し方のまねをする」.
Saying to someone's face 「いい人のふりをしている」 or 「知らないふりしないで」 amounts to accusing them of hypocrisy; it is very strong, so use it with care.
「見て見ぬふり」 is “seeing but acting as if you didn't”, and carries a criticism of “standing by and not taking responsibility”, heavier than 「見ないふり」.
The connection is the same as for an ordinary noun: 「の」 after a noun, 「な」 after a na-adjective: ✕「医者ふりをする」→ ○「医者のふりをする」, ✕「元気ふり」→ ○「元気なふり」.

daily.title: Avoiding being bothered
daily.description: On the train, someone pretends to sleep so they don't have to give up their seat.
daily.example: That person is pretending to be asleep.

daily.title: Keeping a surprise
daily.description: You know about the birthday party but act as if you don't.
daily.example: Let's pretend we don't know about the surprise.

daily.title: Watching the news
daily.description: A news report about a scam.
daily.example: Watch out for scams where people call pretending to be bank employees.

work.title: Attitude in a meeting
work.description: Colleagues privately comment on what happened in a meeting.
work.example: The department head acted like he understood, but I don't think he really did.

work.title: Compliance training
work.description: Company training stresses that you must not ignore violations.
work.example: Turning a blind eye to misconduct is not allowed.

etymology: 「ふり」 is written 「振り」 and comes from the masu-stem of 「振る」 (to swing, to wave). It originally meant body movement or posture (as in 「身振り」, gesture). From “outward appearance” it came to mean “a put-on appearance”, giving 「ふりをする」.

similar.title: 〜ぶる
similar.explanation: 「〜ぶる」 also means putting on an act, but it attaches only to a few nouns and adjectives (「上品ぶる」「先輩ぶる」) and specifically means putting on airs, with a more negative tone. 「〜ふりをする」 attaches to verbs, has wide usage, and isn't necessarily negative.

similar.title: 〜たつもり
similar.explanation: 「〜たつもり」 is a conviction in one's own mind, not necessarily shown to others; 「〜ふりをする」 is deliberately putting on an appearance so that others believe it.

similar.title: 〜てみせる
similar.explanation: 「〜てみせる」 is also “doing it for others to see” (「泣いてみせる」), but the action is really carried out; 「〜ふりをする」 stresses that “it isn't really so, it's just an act”.

formation: It is the noun 「ふり（振り）」 + 「を」 + 「する」. 「ふり」 comes from the continuative form of the verb 「振る」 (to wave), and originally meant bodily movement or posture (as in 「身振り」 and 「素振り」); 「Xふり」 is “the appearance or manner of X”. Add 「をする」 and it is “to put on the look of X”. Because it is only an outward “look”, it implies that “inside it isn't so”, which is how it comes to mean “pretend”. Since 「ふり」 is a noun, what precedes it connects like any ordinary noun modifier: a plain-form verb directly, 「の」 after a noun, 「な」 after a na-adjective. In speech, 「を」 is often dropped to give 「ふりする」.

meaning: Used for prayers and good wishes: “may ...”, “I hope ...”. Also used in letters and official notices to make polite requests.
connection: Verb masu-form + ように (negative: 〜ませんように)

senses.label: Prayer
senses.meaning: A wish made to the gods or in your heart: “please let ...”, “may ...”. Often with 「どうか」 or 「どうぞ」, and written on shrine ema plaques or Tanabata wish strips.
senses.connection: （どうか）verb masu-form + ように (often in the potential form: 合格できますように)
examples: Please let me pass the exam.
May my whole family stay healthy.

senses.label: Wishing others well
senses.meaning: Ends a letter or card with a good wish for the reader: “wishing you ...”, “may you ...”. Often used with honorific language; the tone is formal and warm.
senses.connection: (honorific) verb masu-form + ように (common: お過ごしになれますように, なりますように)
examples: Wishing you a wonderful year.
I sincerely hope you make a speedy recovery.

senses.label: Please don't let ...
senses.meaning: 「〜ませんように」 prays that something bad won't happen: “I hope it doesn't ...”.
senses.connection: Negative verb masu-form + ように (〜ませんように)
examples: Please don't let it rain on tomorrow's sports day.
Please, don't let anyone find me.

senses.label: Polite request
senses.meaning: 「〜くださいますよう（に）お願いいたします」 is a polite request in official notices: “we kindly ask that you ...”. Here 「に」 is often dropped.
senses.connection: 〜くださいます／いただけます + よう（に） + お願い申し上げます・お願いいたします
examples: Please take care not to leave any belongings behind.
We kindly ask that you submit it by the deadline.

notes: A negative wish takes 「ません」: ✕「雨が降らないますように」→ ○「雨が降りませんように」.
When asking someone to do something, use honorifics such as 「くださいますよう」 or 「いただきますよう」: ✕「ご連絡しますようお願いします」 (a humble form wrongly applied to the other person) → ○「ご連絡くださいますようお願いいたします」.
「〜ますように」 only expresses a wish and can't be used to order someone: 「早く寝ますように」 doesn't mean “go to sleep now” but “may I get to bed early”.
The content of the wish should be something you can't directly control, and it often takes the potential form or an intransitive verb (「合格できますように」「晴れますように」).

daily.title: New Year's shrine visit
daily.description: Making a wish at a shrine at New Year.
daily.example: May this year be a good one too.

daily.title: Tanabata wish
daily.description: Writing a wish on a paper strip for Tanabata.
daily.example: I hope I get better at the piano.

daily.title: Writing a card
daily.description: The closing line of a birthday card to a friend.
daily.example: Wishing you a happy year ahead.

work.title: Closing a business email
work.description: A good wish after the seasonal greetings.
work.example: We sincerely wish you all a fruitful year.

work.title: Posting a notice
work.description: A formal notice from a company or a train station.
work.example: We apologize for the inconvenience during construction and kindly ask for your understanding.

etymology: Made of the polite auxiliary 「ます」 plus 「ように」, which expresses purpose or a wish. 「ように」 comes from 「様（よう）」 + 「に」, meaning “so that it becomes like that”. Leaving out a verb like 「祈る」 or 「願う」 after it turns it into a prayer.

similar.title: 〜といい・〜たらいい (wish)
similar.explanation: 「〜といいですね」 also expresses hope, but is a light good wish said to others in everyday conversation; 「〜ますように」 is more solemn and ceremonial, mostly used in making wishes, greeting cards, and letters.

similar.title: 〜てほしい・〜てもらいたい
similar.explanation: 「〜てほしい」 says directly “I want someone to do ...” to a definite person, and toward a superior it feels imposing; 「〜ますように」 is a prayer to the gods or fate that doesn't specify who acts, and is therefore softer.

similar.title: 〜ように (purpose)
similar.explanation: Same origin: the purpose 「〜ように」 means “so that one can ...” and is followed by a real action (「忘れないようにメモする」); drop that following action and replace it with a prayer, and you get 「〜ますように」.

similar.title: 〜ように言う (indirect command)
similar.explanation: Same origin: 「〜ように言う／お願いする」 reports or makes a request (「早く来るように言った」); the 「〜くださいますようお願いいたします」 of official documents is this structure with an honorific and 「ます」 added.

formation: It is the polite auxiliary 「ます」 + 「ように」, with a verb such as 「祈ります」, 「願っています」, or 「お願いします」 omitted after it. 「ように」 comes from 「様（よう）＋に」 and means “so as to become that state”; it is a “goal” marker. The full phrase 「〜ますように（と祈ります）」 is “I pray that things become ...”. Because it expresses a state one hopes to reach, the content is often something you can't control directly, so the potential form or an intransitive verb is common. 「ます」 rarely survives inside an ordinary subordinate clause, but is deliberately kept here, giving the wish itself a formal tone and thus a ceremonial feel suited to making wishes and greeting cards. Replace the omitted verb with 「お願いいたします」 and add honorifics like 「くださる」, and it becomes the formal request of official documents, 「〜くださいますようお願いいたします」.

meaning: Expresses a judgment based on a feeling, without solid evidence: “I have a feeling that ...”, “it seems to me that ...”.
connection: Verb / adjective plain form, na-adjective + な, noun + の + ような気がする

senses.label: I have a feeling
senses.meaning: An uncertain judgment based on intuition: “I have a feeling ...”, “somehow it seems ...”. The tone is soft; often used with 「なんだか」 or 「なんとなく」.
senses.connection: Plain form + ような気がする (common: なんとなく〜ような気がする)
examples: Somehow I have a feeling something good will happen today.
I feel like I've been down this road before.

senses.label: Softening an opinion
senses.meaning: Presents your opinion as just a feeling, avoiding a firm statement and softening the tone. Often used to point out a problem or to disagree.
senses.connection: Plain form + ような気がする／ような気がします（けど）
examples: I feel that explanation might be a little off...
I feel like this design is a bit too flashy.

senses.label: Casual / short forms
senses.meaning: In conversation, 「〜みたいな気がする」 is common, and 「ような」 can be dropped to say just 「〜気がする」, with the same meaning.
senses.connection: Plain form + みたいな気がする／気がする (common: 〜た気がする, 〜ない気がする)
examples: I feel like I've met that person somewhere.
I have a feeling he won't come.

notes: The subject is the speaker. To describe someone else's feeling, use 「〜ような気がするそうだ」, 「〜と感じているようだ」, and the like.
「気がする」, 「気にする」, and 「気になる」 differ by only one particle but mean quite different things: 「気がする」 = “to feel / have a feeling”; 「気にする」 = “to worry about”; 「気になる」 = “to be on one's mind / curious”.
「〜気がしない」 has two meanings: 「負ける気がしない」 = “I don't feel I'll lose”; 「食べる気がしない」 = “I don't feel like eating”. Tell them apart by context.

Where a clear answer is needed (when asked to confirm something or commit to a deadline), answering only 「〜ような気がします」 is seen in Japanese workplaces as irresponsible. State the facts clearly or say plainly 「確認いたします」.
A noun takes 「の」 and a na-adjective takes 「な」: ✕「夢ような気がする」→ ○「夢のような気がする」.

daily.title: Déjà vu
daily.description: You're somewhere for the first time but it feels familiar, and you tell a friend.
daily.example: It's my first time here, but somehow it feels nostalgic.

daily.title: Feeling unwell
daily.description: You think you might be coming down with a cold.
daily.example: I somehow feel like I have a fever.

work.title: Gently pointing out a problem
work.description: Raising a concern about a colleague's plan in a meeting.
work.example: With this schedule, I feel it might be a bit unrealistic.

work.title: Checking a fact
work.description: You can't remember clearly whether you received a document.
work.example: I have a feeling I received those materials last week...

etymology: 「ような」 is the attributive form of the auxiliary 「ようだ」 (likeness), and 「気がする」 means “to have a feeling” (「気」 means mind or feeling). Together: “to have a feeling that it's like ...”.

similar.title: 〜ようだ・〜みたいだ
similar.explanation: Same origin: the 「ような」 in this grammar point is the attributive form of 「ようだ」. 「〜ようだ」 is a guess based on observed facts and has some grounds; 「〜ような気がする」 is just a feeling, more subjective and less certain.

similar.title: 〜と思う (I think)
similar.explanation: 「〜と思う」 is your own judgment or opinion and is fairly definite; 「〜ような気がする」 recasts the judgment as a “feeling”, which is softer and less certain, suited to when you don't want to commit.

similar.title: 〜がする (feeling)
similar.explanation: Same origin: 「〜がする」 expresses a sensory perception (「音がする」「いい匂いがする」); 「気がする」 is “feeling it in the mind”, an extension of this usage.

similar.title: 〜かもしれない
similar.explanation: 「〜かもしれない」 objectively says “it's possible”; 「〜ような気がする」 is subjective intuition, where the speaker just “vaguely feels” it is so.

formation: It is 「ような」 (the attributive form of the comparative auxiliary 「ようだ」, “like ...”) + 「気」 (mind, feeling) + 「が」 + 「する」. 「〜がする」 originally expresses sensing a sound or smell (「音がする」「匂いがする」), so 「気がする」 is “a feeling arises in the mind”. Modifying that feeling with 「ような」 shows it is only “a feeling that it seems like ...” and not a confirmed judgment; two layers of uncertainty are stacked, making the tone especially soft. It therefore suits expressing intuition and is also often used to soften one's own opinion. Dropping 「ような」 and saying just 「〜気がする」 is also fine, but loses the layer of “it seems”.

meaning: Says that, judging from outward appearance, something looks a certain way: “looks like ...”, “seems ...”.
connection: Verb / adjective plain form, na-adjective + な, noun + の + ように見える

senses.label: Looks ... (guess)
senses.meaning: Judging from appearance, something seems to be in a certain state: “looks ...”, “appears to ...”. It may not actually be true.
senses.connection: Verb te-iru form・ta-form・plain form + ように見える
examples: He looks tired.
Those two seem to get along well.

senses.label: Looks like (simile)
senses.meaning: Sees one thing as another: “looks just like ...”. Usually 「noun + のように見える」.
senses.connection: Noun + の + ように見える
examples: From here, the clouds look like cotton candy.
This painting looks like a photograph.

senses.label: Doesn't look ...
senses.meaning: The negative 「〜ようには見えない」 means “doesn't look ... at all”, often with surprise or doubt.
senses.connection: Plain form + ようには見えない／ように見えない
examples: She doesn't look anywhere near fifty.
He didn't look like he was sorry at all.

notes: A na-adjective takes 「な」 and a noun takes 「の」: ✕「元気ように見える」→ ○「元気なように見える」.
When used about appearance, 「五十歳のようには見えない」 is a compliment, but 「やる気があるようには見えない」 is criticism, and rude to say to someone's face.
「見える」 is intransitive (“look, seem”) and 「見せる」 is transitive (“make it look”): 「忙しいように見える」 = “looks busy”; 「忙しいように見せる」 = “deliberately act busy”.
「〜ように見える」 only expresses an outward impression and doesn't guarantee the facts. For a confident judgment use 「〜に違いない」 and the like; don't state how it looks as if it were a conclusion.

daily.title: Worrying about a friend
daily.description: Asking a friend who looks pale if they're OK.
daily.example: You look pale. It looks like you have a fever. Are you OK?

daily.title: Enjoying the view
daily.description: Looking at the night view from a mountaintop.
daily.example: The city lights look like stars, don't they?

work.title: Market analysis
work.description: Analyzing data trends in a meeting.
work.example: At first glance, sales seem to be recovering, but they're actually flat.

work.title: News report
work.description: A news commentary on a situation.
work.example: Relations between the two countries appear to be improving.

etymology: Made of 「ように」, the adverbial form of the auxiliary 「ようだ」, plus the verb 「見える」 (to look, to appear): “to look like that”.

similar.title: 〜く見える・〜に見える
similar.explanation: Same origin: 「若く見える」 and 「学生に見える」 attach directly to an adjective or noun and describe only the plain appearance; 「〜ように見える」 can take a whole sentence (「疲れているように見える」) and express more complex situations.

similar.title: 〜そうだ (appearance)
similar.explanation: 「〜そうだ」 judges directly from appearance (「おいしそうだ」「雨が降りそうだ」) and is mostly an immediate impression at a glance; 「〜ように見える」 is a more objective observation and often implies “it may not actually be so”.

similar.title: 〜ようだ・〜みたいだ
similar.explanation: Same origin: 「〜ようだ」 can guess from various signs (things heard or felt); 「〜ように見える」 limits the basis to “how it looks”.

similar.title: 〜とみえる
similar.explanation: Same origin: both use 「見える」. 「〜とみえる」 is more written, and guesses another's state from signs (「よほど疲れているとみえる」); 「〜ように見える」 is used in both speech and writing, and focuses on describing an outward impression.

formation: It is 「ように」 (the adverbial form of the comparative auxiliary 「ようだ」, “in the way that ...”) + the intransitive verb 「見える」 (to come into view, to appear). 「ようだ」 is already a guess of “it seems that ...”; adding 「見える」 explicitly limits the basis of the judgment to a “visual impression”. Since it is only “how it looks”, it doesn't guarantee it is so, and it is often set against 「本当は」 or 「実は」; the negative 「ようには見えない」 stresses “you can't tell at all from the outside”. The 「よう」 before it comes from the noun 「様」, so a noun takes 「の」 and a na-adjective takes 「な」.

meaning: Uses 「まるで」 to strengthen a simile: “just like ...”, “as if ...”. Compares something to a different thing.
connection: まるで + verb / adjective plain form, noun + の + ようだ・ような・ように (casual: みたいだ)

senses.label: Just like ... (end of sentence)
senses.meaning: It isn't really so, but it looks very much like something: “it's just like ...”. 「まるで」 stresses how similar it is.
senses.connection: まるで + noun + の／plain form + ようだ・ようです
examples: This room is just like a hotel.
I can't believe I passed. It's like a dream.

senses.label: Modifying nouns and verbs
senses.meaning: 「まるで〜ような + noun」 modifies a noun; 「まるで〜ように + verb」 modifies an action: “a ... just like ...”, “... just as if ...”.
senses.connection: まるで + 〜ような + noun／まるで + 〜ように + verb・adjective
examples: It was a smile just like a child's.
She speaks Japanese just like a native speaker.

senses.label: Casual 「みたい」
senses.meaning: In conversation, 「まるで〜みたいだ／みたいな／みたいに」 is common. The meaning is the same, but more casual.
senses.connection: まるで + noun／plain form + みたいだ・みたいな・みたいに
examples: It's so hot today, it's just like summer.
That dog laughs just like a human.

notes: When 「まるで」 is followed by a negative it means “not at all”: 「まるで分からない」 = “I don't understand at all”, not a simile.
It is used only for similes where it isn't actually so, never for guesses: ✕「空が暗い。まるで雨が降るようだ」→ ○「雨が降りそうだ」.
「まるで」 must be matched by 「ようだ／みたいだ」, not 「らしい」 or 「そうだ」: ✕「まるで夢らしい」→ ○「まるで夢のようだ」.
Saying 「まるで子どもみたい」 to an adult criticizes them as childish, and is very rude to a superior or customer.

daily.title: Sightseeing
daily.description: Exclaiming at beautiful scenery.
daily.example: This view looks just like a postcard.

daily.title: Praising a child
daily.description: Noticing how grown-up a child has become.
daily.example: You talk just like a grown-up.

daily.title: Reading a novel
daily.description: A description you come across in a novel.
daily.example: The sky was red, as if it were on fire.

work.title: News report
work.description: Reporting on a disaster area.
work.example: The disaster area looked just like a battlefield.

work.title: Product promotion
work.description: An ad describing how realistic a product is.
work.example: Enjoy a texture just like the real thing.

etymology: 「まるで」 comes from 「まる」 of the adjective 「丸い」 (round) plus the particle 「で」. It originally meant “completely, entirely”, which led to the emphatic simile use (“just like”) and the use with negatives (“not at all”).

similar.title: 〜かのようだ
similar.explanation: 「まるで〜かのようだ」 stresses “as if it were really so (when it isn't)”, often takes a whole sentence (「まるで何もなかったかのように」), and is more written; 「まるで〜ようだ」 is used in both speech and writing.

similar.title: 〜ようだ・〜みたいだ
similar.explanation: Same origin: 「〜ようだ」 on its own mostly expresses a guess (「誰か来たようだ」); adding 「まるで」 pins it down as a simile (it actually isn't so).

similar.title: 〜ような・〜ように・〜みたいな (simile / example)
similar.explanation: Same origin: 「〜のような・〜のように」 can express a simile by itself (「雪のような白い肌」); 「まるで」 just intensifies the resemblance, making the simile more exaggerated and vivid.

formation: It is the adverb 「まるで」 (originally “completely, entirely”) + the comparative auxiliary 「ようだ／みたいだ」. 「ようだ」 can express both a guess and a simile; putting 「まるで」 at the head announces that “the resemblance that follows is ‘complete’”, and saying “exactly like” tacitly means “in fact it isn't”, which locks the meaning to a simile. When the “completely” of 「まるで」 pairs with a negative it becomes “not at all” (「まるで分からない」), which is why the two uses come from one word. The inflected forms 「ような／ように」 of 「ようだ」 modify a noun and a verb respectively, so 「まるで〜」 can also serve as an attributive or an adverbial.

meaning: Makes a guess based on what you can see or on clues: “it seems ...”, “apparently ...”. Mostly about other people's states; somewhat formal.
connection: Verb / adjective plain form, noun・na-adjective (+ だ) + とみえる・とみえて

senses.label: It seems ... (end of sentence)
senses.meaning: Makes a guess from facts or signs in front of you: “it seems ...”. A sentence giving the evidence often comes before or after, and the subject is usually a third person.
senses.connection: Plain form + とみえる (often with 「よほど」 or 「かなり」)
examples: He must be extremely tired.
There's always a line at that restaurant. It must be really good.

senses.label: Seems ..., so ...
senses.meaning: 「〜とみえて」 in mid-sentence states the guess first, then the evidence: “apparently ..., because ...”.
senses.connection: Plain form + とみえて、〜
examples: The child must have been tired; he fell asleep right away.
It seems it rained last night; the road is wet.

senses.label: 「ものとみえる」
senses.meaning: 「〜ものとみえる」 is a more formal version with a slightly serious tone, common in reports and commentary.
senses.connection: Plain form + ものとみえる／ものとみられる
examples: It appears the culprit got in through the window.
He appears to be against that plan.

notes: The thing guessed about is another person or a situation; it is unnatural about yourself: ✕「私は疲れているとみえる」→ ○「（私は）疲れているようだ」.
「よほど暇とみえるね」 and 「よほど自信があるとみえる」 are often used sarcastically; said in front of the person they sound condescending and mocking, which is rude.
In 「〜とみえて、〜」 the second clause is the phenomenon that serves as evidence, not the result: 「疲れたとみえて、すぐ寝た」 = “he must have been tired, (since) he fell asleep right away”.
When written 「と見える」, don't confuse it with 「〜が見える」 or 「はっきりと見える」 (“can be seen”): 「山がはっきりと見える」 is vision, not a guess.

daily.title: Watching a family member
daily.description: A family member says nothing, and you guess how they feel.
daily.example: Dad isn't saying a word. He must be really angry.

daily.title: Reading a novel
daily.description: Appears in a novel describing a character's expression.
daily.example: She seemed nervous; her voice was trembling.

work.title: News report
work.description: A report makes a guess from signs at the scene.
work.example: The fire appears to have started in the kitchen.

work.title: Analysis report
work.description: Guessing the cause from data.
work.example: The new product seems to have a good reputation; inquiries have shot up.

etymology: Made of the quoting particle 「と」 plus the verb 「見える」 (to look, to appear), literally “it looks like ...”. From visual “appearing” it came to mean “it seems”, a guess based on signs.

similar.title: 〜らしい
similar.explanation: 「〜らしい」 guesses from hearsay or indirect information and is common in speech; 「〜とみえる」 guesses from signs you see before your eyes, is more written, and often has the tone of an onlooker commenting.

similar.title: 〜とみられる
similar.explanation: Same origin: 「〜とみられる」 is the passive of 「みる」, mostly used in news, meaning “is thought to be / is presumed”, with an objective tone; 「〜とみえる」 is the speaker's own guess.

similar.title: 〜ところを見ると
similar.explanation: 「〜ところを見ると」 states the grounds first and then the guess (「笑っているところを見ると、合格したようだ」); 「〜とみえる」 gives the guess first, and the grounds can go before or after.

similar.title: 〜ように見える
similar.explanation: Same origin: 「〜ように見える」 only describes an outward impression (“looks like”); 「〜とみえる」 draws a conclusion from signs (“it seems that ...”), and has a stronger sense of inference.

formation: It is the quotative particle 「と」 + the intransitive verb 「見える」 (to seem, to look). 「と」 brings up the preceding judgment as a piece of content, so literally “(things) look as ‘...’”: the speaker frames the conclusion read from signs with 「と」, marking it as “a conclusion arrived at by observation”, not a fact confirmed first-hand. 「見える」 is intransitive and its subject is the situation itself, giving the feel of a bystander calmly commenting on another person or a situation, so it is unnatural about oneself, and in front of the person concerned it easily seems aloof. In the continuative 「とみえて」 it becomes “it seems ..., so ...”, linking the guess to the phenomenon that serves as evidence.
